<reason>Side B (PRO) won a close but clear debate. Its core route — that manufacturers shrink packages precisely because the sticker is read and the gram count is not — was strengthened, not neutralized, when Side A conceded in A2.2 that firms shrink "to preserve price points consumers anchor on." B exploited this concession relentlessly (B4.1, B5.1) and answered A's memory-parity pressure question with a real distinction: the sticker is actively read and comparable to the rival brand beside it, while the gram count never changes appearance. B also handled A's delta-mixing pressure with a workable fix (show two lines) plus the receipt-total analogy, and its "retreat narrative" (B4.5-4.6) framed A's successive objections as implicit concessions that shoppers aren't seeing the change today. Side A landed real hits — the baseline problem genuinely forced B to modify its one-line flag, and the "universal price-history regime" scope-creep charge had teeth given B's "I won't object" concession on was-$3.49 tags. But B's replies kept the core case intact: a temporary flag on a minority of items, at the sticker the shopper does read, is not the permanent fine print A's fatigue argument assumes. Both sides used Q1/Q2 and A1/A2 formats correctly; both had clipped turns, so no asymmetrical execution cost. B made the debate easier to decide and held the decisive live route throughout.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The exchange around A's Q2 (the "unit price up 11%" that bundles a 5% price rise with a 6% size cut). A scored a genuine hit by showing B's opening flag misattributes causes, but B's answer — "show both lines: size down 6%, price up 5%, cost per gram up 11%," plus the receipt-total point that the composite is what the shopper actually pays — neutralized the objection while A's follow-up that this "concedes the baseline point" was the sharpest CON moment of the debate.</best_rebuttal>
